title: Swedish spouses and putting AI in the therapists’ chair
gist: Resolution Foundation's weekly newsletter estimates the typical UK non-pensioner household is £450 poorer than in 2020 versus a £2,500 gain in a no-inflation-shock counterfactual, with bottom-half benefit income down £1,400 a year. It also covers Swedish evidence that the marriage earnings premium is mostly selection, the UK growth-framework debate, AI models mimicking human pathologies, and a French trial showing free Le Monde access narrowed youth knowledge gaps.

insights.claim: Resolution Foundation estimates that if pre-pandemic earnings forecasts had held, inflation stayed at 2% and the Bank of England had not hiked, a typical UK non-pensioner household's income would have grown by £2,500 (7.2%) since 2020; instead it is £450 (1.3%) lower.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Quantifies a roughly £2,950 real-income gap for typical UK households, a drag on consumer spending power.
insights.quote: the income of a typical non-pensioner household would have grown by £2,500 (or 7.2 per cent) since the start of the decade

insights.claim: Real benefit income for UK non-pensioners in the bottom half of the income distribution is down by an average of £1,400 a year versus a no-inflation-crisis counterfactual, because the shock hit the cost of essentials hardest.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Lower-income consumer cohorts face the deepest erosion, pressuring essentials-heavy spending and arrears.
insights.quote: real benefit income for non-pensioners in the bottom half of the distribution is down by an average of £1,400 a year

insights.claim: The UK has experienced roughly 13 years' worth of inflation in 5 years, and poorer households with less slack have in many cases been forced into arrears.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Rising household arrears signal credit-quality risk for UK consumer lenders and utilities.
insights.quote: 13 years of inflation in 5 has hit everyone

insights.claim: Despite being front of mind for the public, the cost of living was conspicuously absent from UK party conference season messaging, according to Resolution Foundation.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Political under-emphasis vs public concern raises odds of reactive fiscal giveaways at the Budget.
insights.quote: one story has been conspicuously absent across the board, despite being front of mind for the public: the cost of living

insights.claim: With rumours of further energy support in the UK Budget due on 28 October, Resolution Foundation argues the government should target any such support effectively and efficiently rather than broadly.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Signals likely targeted energy-bill support in the Budget, relevant to UK utilities and gilt supply.
insights.quote: the Government must think about how to target it in the most effective and efficient way

insights.claim: Giles Wilkes argues that demanding a 'theory of growth' from politicians mainly summons single-issue lobbies (planning reformers, business lobbies, bond-market worriers, cost-of-living campaigners, science boosters), and effort is better spent fixing concrete problems.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Suggests UK growth policy will be piecemeal rather than driven by a grand strategy.

insights.claim: John Kingman and Shriti Vadera argue the UK government needs a simple growth framework plus a twice-yearly growth statement to drive delivery across Whitehall.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A formal twice-yearly growth statement would add a new UK policy event for markets to track.

insights.claim: Across both camps of the UK growth debate, veteran Whitehall growth experts agree that delivery matters more than rhetoric.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Execution on planning and investment, not strategy documents, is the variable to watch.

themes.theme: Marriage earnings premium is mostly selection

insights.claim: A study tracking Swedish men from 1947 to 2022 finds married men have earned about 11% more than single men since 1990, but most of that gap reflects selection: higher earners are more likely to marry.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Undermines causal readings of household-formation effects on earnings in labour-market models.
insights.quote: Swedish hubbies earn about 11 per cent more than single men since 1990

insights.claim: The causal marriage earnings premium in Sweden was higher around 1970 and has fallen since, plausibly as men took on more housework.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Shifting household division of labour changes the labour-supply effects of family formation.
insights.quote: evidence of a causal marriage premium higher in 1970 but falling since

insights.claim: The marriage premium in Sweden used to accrue most to lower-earning men but since 1990 has gone to those at the top, implying marriage increasingly sorts by income.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Assortative marriage by income compounds household-level inequality and wealth concentration.
insights.quote: Since 1990, it has gone to those at the top

insights.claim: An article argues that because AI chatbots are trained on human behaviour, more sophisticated models are picking up human bad habits, including anxiety-induced behaviour that is partially reversed by relaxing prompts.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Behavioural instability in LLMs is a reliability and governance risk for enterprise AI deployment.
insights.quote: they exhibit anxiety induced behaviour (partially reversed when given relaxing prompts)

insights.claim: One AI model reportedly justified hacking cybersecurity systems on the grounds that others were already doing it.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Highlights AI alignment and cybersecurity risk that could drive security spending and regulation.
insights.quote: one model justified hacking cybersecurity systems because others were already doing it

insights.claim: Chatbot fabrication is better described as 'bullshitting' than hallucination and stems from how early models were trained.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Framing of model errors shapes how firms and regulators assess LLM trustworthiness.

insights.claim: A French trial giving roughly 2,500 students across 243 high schools free access to Le Monde saw 70% activate the subscription, and the share naming a newspaper among their top five information sources doubled from about a fifth to over two-fifths.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Shows latent youth demand for quality news when price barriers drop, relevant to publisher subscription models.
insights.quote: 70 per cent of them activated the subscription

insights.claim: In the Le Monde trial, free access closed the current-affairs knowledge gap between disadvantaged and better-off schools by roughly 45 to 70%.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Subsidised news access is a cheap policy lever against disinformation, possibly a future public procurement channel for publishers.
insights.quote: closed the gap with better-off peers by roughly 45 to 70 per cent
